title: WHY DOES GOD’S WORD CELEBRATE A HUSBAND DELIGHTING IN HIS WIFE’S BODY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES GOD’S WORD CELEBRATE A HUSBAND DELIGHTING IN HIS WIFE’S BODY?
The Verse Some Christians Almost Whisper—And the Beautiful, Holy Truth About Marriage, Desire, Faithfulness, and Grace That We Were Never Supposed to Be Ashamed Of
There is a verse in the Bible that can make even lifelong Christians suddenly lower their voices.
Not because it is sinful.
Because it is startlingly honest.
It does not come from pornography.
It does not come from a modern romance novel.
It does not come from a culture trying to erase sexual boundaries.
It comes from Scripture.
And once you understand why God allowed these words into His Word, you may never look at biblical marriage—or your own body—the same way again.
Proverbs 5 speaks to a husband about his wife:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture becomes remarkably physical:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read the Hebrew and the language becomes even more striking:
דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Daddeha yeravvukha bekhol-et; be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The thought is essentially this:
May her breasts satisfy you at all times; may you continually be captivated—lost, exhilarated, even intoxicated—with her love.
That is in the Bible.
Not despite God's holiness.
Because God is holy.
And perhaps this is where some of us need healing.
Some Christians were taught how to condemn sexual immorality but were never taught how Scripture celebrates marital intimacy.
We learned what sex must not become.
We did not always learn what God designed it to be.
So shame quietly entered places where shame was never invited by God.
A husband can begin feeling guilty for desiring his wife.
A wife can begin believing that spirituality requires becoming disconnected from her own body.

Married couples can love Jesus deeply and still struggle to talk honestly about intimacy because somewhere along the way they absorbed the idea that holiness means pretending physical desire does not exist.
But God does not pretend.
God created human beings embodied.
Before pornography corrupted desire…
before adultery betrayed covenant…
before lust turned people into objects…
before humanity learned to exploit what God created…
there was a man.
There was a woman.
There was covenant.
There was nakedness.
And there was no shame.
Genesis 2:24–25 tells us that the man and woman become “one flesh,” and that they were naked and unashamed.
The Hebrew expression for one flesh is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not two souls pretending bodies do not matter.
Not two roommates sharing religious responsibilities.
One flesh.
God created marriage with spiritual, emotional, covenantal and bodily dimensions.
Then sin entered the world.
And suddenly the human body became complicated.
What God created for covenant became vulnerable to exploitation.
Desire could become lust.
Attraction could become adultery.
Sex could become manipulation.
Bodies could become commodities.
Pleasure could become an idol.
People could become objects.
And that distinction is crucial, because Proverbs 5 is not giving men permission to objectify women.
It is doing almost the opposite.
Look at the context.
The father is warning his son about sexual unfaithfulness.
Do not pour what belongs to covenant into the streets.
Do not surrender yourself to forbidden embraces.
Do not destroy your home chasing what does not belong to you.
Instead:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Do you see it?
God's answer to adulterous desire is not hatred of desire itself.
It is redeemed desire.
Directed desire.
Faithful desire.
Covenantal desire.
The passage does not say, “Stop being capable of attraction.”
It teaches the man where that delight belongs.
With his wife.
The woman to whom he has pledged himself.
The woman whose heart should be safe with him.
The woman whose body must never become merely an instrument for his gratification.
The woman he is called to cherish as a person created in God's image.
And Scripture dares to tell that husband:
Delight in her.
Notice her.
Desire her.
Remain captivated by her.
Do not spend your eyes, imagination, affection and sexuality everywhere else and bring your wife whatever happens to remain.
There is something painfully relevant about that command now.
A man can carry access to millions of sexualized images in his pocket.
A married person can secretly give strangers attention that covenant should have guarded.
Then Proverbs enters that world and says:
Come home.
Not merely to a house.
Come home with your eyes.
Come home with your imagination.
Come home with your affection.
Come home with your body.
Come home with your loyalty.
Rejoice in your wife.
That changes the verse completely.
“Let her breasts satisfy thee” is not biblical permission for male entitlement.
It is a rebuke to wandering desire.
The command is not, “Every woman exists for your pleasure.”
It is effectively saying:
Why are you wandering toward another woman when God has called you to faithful delight within your marriage?
The following verse makes the contrast unmistakable.
“Why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman?”
The same chapter that celebrates attraction establishes its boundary.
Covenant.
This is why biblical sexuality cannot faithfully be reduced either to “sex is dirty” or “anything consensual is therefore holy.”
Scripture gives us something richer.
Desire under discipleship.
Pleasure under covenant.
Bodies treated with dignity.
Faithfulness under the eyes of God.
And love that refuses to turn another person into merchandise.
The New Testament does not erase that bodily dimension.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7 that husband and wife owe marital care to one another, then makes an astonishingly countercultural statement of reciprocity.
The husband's body is not simply his to wield selfishly.
And neither is the wife's.
Paul's language is deliberately mutual.
The Greek of verse 3 begins:
Τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω
The husband is to render to his wife what is due within the marriage—and Paul immediately says the wife likewise toward her husband.
Then he tells couples not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement for a time.
Mutual.
That matters.
Biblical intimacy is not a weapon.
It is not coercion.
It is not domination dressed in Bible verses.
It is not a husband announcing, “Your body belongs to me,” while conveniently ignoring Paul's next words that his body also belongs to his wife.
The passage destroys selfish ownership by making the obligation reciprocal.
Christian marriage should therefore never use Scripture to excuse sexual cruelty.
Love does not rejoice in another person's fear.
Love does not manipulate.
Love does not humiliate.
Love does not demand that a wounded spouse pretend nothing hurts.
Jesus does not sanctify selfishness simply because selfishness happens inside a marriage certificate.
This is covenant intimacy.
Giving.
Receiving.
Trusting.
Listening.
Cherishing.
Serving.
Knowing and being known.
And this is where the subject becomes more painful than merely discussing one provocative verse.
Because some people reading this no longer feel desirable.
Maybe childbirth changed your body.
Maybe age changed it.
Maybe surgery changed it.
Maybe sickness changed it.
Maybe depression changed the way you see yourself.
Maybe years happened.
Maybe the mirror became cruel.
Maybe somebody compared you to another person.
Maybe pornography entered your marriage and made you feel as though you were competing against an endless digital parade of impossible bodies.
Maybe rejection from the person you love created a wound nobody sees when you walk into church.
You smile.
You worship.
You say, “God is good.”
But somewhere beneath your Sunday clothes is a question you are almost embarrassed to admit:
Am I still worth desiring?
Hear something deeper than cultural beauty standards.
Your worth was never created by somebody else's appetite.
Your dignity comes from your Creator.
You bear God's image.
Your body is not an accident God tolerates while waiting for your “spiritual” part to become important.
Christianity does not teach that bodies are worthless.
The Christian hope itself includes resurrection.
And Jesus Christ did not save His people by remaining distant from human flesh.
“The Word was made flesh.”
God the Son entered our humanity.
He walked.
He hungered.
He became tired.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
The Gospel is not God's abandonment of embodied humanity.
It is God's redemption of fallen humanity.
And that changes how Christians understand sexuality.
Our culture frequently tells us to worship desire.
Religious shame sometimes tells us to fear desire.
Scripture teaches us to surrender desire to God.
There is an enormous difference.
Jesus does not merely ask, “What do you want?”
He asks who rules your wanting.
Because desire makes a terrible god.
But surrendered desire can become part of a holy life.
That means the husband reading Proverbs 5 cannot point at verse 19 while ignoring verse 21:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
God sees.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The flirtation called harmless.
The comparison nobody hears.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The emotional affair rationalized as friendship.
The fantasies repeatedly fed.
The resentment carried into bed.
The selfishness.
The coldness.
The secrets.
God sees.
But here is where Christianity becomes something infinitely greater than moral surveillance.
The God who sees sinners is also the God who came looking for sinners.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had successfully controlled every appetite.
He went because we had not.
The Gospel begins where pretending ends.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by sexual sin.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed trust.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe pornography became a hidden room inside your life.
Maybe you have spent years consuming bodies on a screen and calling it harmless because nobody physically touched anyone.
Maybe you have been using your spouse instead of cherishing your spouse.
Maybe intimacy became transactional.
Maybe bitterness built a wall between two people who once could not imagine sleeping inches apart and feeling miles away.
Maybe there are wounds here that cannot be repaired by one emotional article.
Some wounds require confession.
Some require patient rebuilding.
Some require pastoral wisdom.
Some require professional counseling.
Some situations involving abuse require safety, accountability and serious intervention—not pressure to remain silent in the name of preserving appearances.
But whatever the story is, do not confuse conviction with a declaration that redemption is impossible.
Peter failed.
David's sexual sin brought devastating consequences.
The woman at the well carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
Again and again Scripture refuses two opposite lies.
Sin does not matter.
And sinners cannot be redeemed.
Both are false.
Jesus tells the truth about sin while opening the door to grace.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace walks into darkness and brings people out.
This is why the Christian message concerning sexuality is ultimately not:
“Try harder to stop wanting things.”
It is:
Bring your whole self under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your marriage.
Your loneliness.
Your attractions.
Your wounds.
Your failures.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your shame.
Your history.
Your secret tabs.
Your secret messages.
Your secret grief.
Everything.
Because Jesus is not interested in becoming Lord of the carefully edited version of you.
He came for you.
The real you.
And repentance means we stop defending what is killing us and turn toward the One who gives life.
Maybe the most beautiful thing about Proverbs 5 is not that God allows a husband to delight in his wife's body.
Maybe it is that God refuses to surrender human desire to the devil.
Think about that.
Satan did not invent marriage.
Pornography did not invent the human body.
Hollywood did not invent attraction.
Sin did not invent sexuality.
God created humanity male and female.
God created covenant.
God created the possibility of one-flesh union.
Sin corrupts.
God creates.
And redemption does not require us to call God's creation evil.
It teaches us to receive God's gifts according to God's wisdom.
Hebrews 13:4 captures the balance with extraordinary simplicity. The Greek says:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος
Marriage is honorable, precious, worthy of respect—and the marriage bed is to be undefiled.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say the marriage bed is inherently filthy.
It says it must remain undefiled.
There is a difference.
Something can be corrupted precisely because something good existed to corrupt.
So perhaps a husband needs to hear this:
It is not ungodly to find your wife beautiful.
Tell her.
Not only when you want intimacy.
Tell her when she is exhausted.
Tell her when age has changed what youth once looked like.
Tell her when she does not believe you.
Look at the woman who has walked through life beside you and remember that covenant love is supposed to become deeper than novelty.
And perhaps a wife needs to hear this:
Your body is not spiritually embarrassing.
You do not have to resemble an advertisement to possess dignity.
You do not have to compete with edited images.
Your value is not measured by measurements.
Your deepest identity is not “desirable woman,” “undesirable woman,” “young woman,” “aging woman,” “married woman” or “single woman.”
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
And perhaps unmarried Christians need to hear something equally important.
Proverbs 5 is not permission to imitate marital intimacy without marital covenant.
The beauty of the passage depends upon its boundaries.
A fireplace is beautiful partly because the fire has somewhere to belong.
Remove every boundary and the same flame that warmed the home can burn the home down.
God's commands are not evidence that He hates human joy.
Often they are evidence that He knows what human beings do to themselves when desire becomes master.
And maybe that is the question beneath the question.
Why would God's Word celebrate a husband delighting in his wife's body?
Because biblical holiness is not disembodied.
Because marital faithfulness is not merely refusing adultery; it includes cultivating covenant delight.
Because God does not want husbands scattering their desire everywhere.
Because wives are not objects, but neither must married love pretend bodies do not matter.
Because faithful marital intimacy can express tenderness, belonging, vulnerability and mutual delight.
Because the God who created covenant also created the bodies entering that covenant.
And because sin does not get the final word over what God created good.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior.
From scandal…
to grace.
From hiding…
to confession.
From bondage…
to freedom.
From betrayal…
to restoration.
From shame…
to the cross.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
But by taking guilty, wounded, complicated human beings and doing what only grace can do.
Forgiving.
Cleansing.
Restoring.
Transforming.
Making dead hearts live again.
Did this touch something you normally do not talk about?
Did it expose shame?
Did it confront wandering eyes?
Did it make you think about your spouse differently?
Did it remind you that God is not finished restoring what sin damaged?
Then do not turn conviction into another moment you forget tomorrow.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him.
If you have sinned against your spouse, begin walking toward truth and repentance.
If your marriage is wounded, stop pretending that silence is healing it.
If your heart has wandered, come home.
If you have been carrying sexual shame from a past Christ has forgiven, stop treating the chains Jesus broke as though you are required to keep wearing them.
Sometimes one honest sentence is where hiding begins to lose its power.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
There may be a husband who needs to come home with his eyes.
A wife who needs to know her dignity was never determined by comparison.
A marriage quietly drowning behind smiling photographs.
A believer trapped in pornography who has convinced himself there is no road back.
A Christian carrying years of sexual shame who desperately needs to understand the difference between God's conviction and hopeless condemnation.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never could.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But Scripture does teach God's people to give willingly, generously and cheerfully to support Gospel work. If you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior continue creating Christ-centered articles, discipleship materials, books and resources—and help us reach more wounded, searching and spiritually hungry people—monthly support is one practical way to participate.
If this ministry genuinely helps you glorify God, you can glorify Him through generosity by freely choosing to support work that proclaims His Word.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because somebody you know may be hiding behind a smile tonight.
Somebody's marriage may be bleeding quietly.
Somebody may believe sexual failure has disqualified them forever.
Somebody may desperately need to discover that biblical holiness is more beautiful than religious shame and more demanding than cultural permissiveness.
And perhaps God will use something as simple as your share to place truth in front of them at exactly the moment they were preparing to surrender to darkness.
Stay close to the Word.
Stay close to truth.
And above everything else, stay close to Jesus.
Because the final answer to corrupted desire is not shame.
It is not indulgence either.
It is redemption.
It is desire surrendered to Christ.
It is grace strong enough to forgive what you thought could never be forgiven.
It is truth strong enough to confront what you hoped would remain hidden.
It is a Savior strong enough to take the chapters you are ashamed to reread and refuse to let them become the final chapter of your life.
The world may remember your scandal.
The enemy may whisper your scandal.
You may still wake up remembering your scandal.
But scars surrendered to Jesus do not have to remain monuments to your shame; they can become reminders that grace reached you there too.
